title: Write: Markdown and DocxXML
p: MarkdownX reads and writes two formats. Markdown is the quick, portable path; DocxXML is the native format and keeps every block, including interactive ones. You can mix them in one book: a chapter can be either.
Type Markdown directly, or paste it from another editor. Headings, lists, tasks, quotes, tables, fenced code and images are recognised on import.

pre.caption: A small chapter
pre.code:
# A small chapter
- one idea per line - **bold** and `code` - [a link](https://example.com)
> A quote can carry the argument.

p: Use # through ###### for headings. A line starting with - becomes a list, - [ ] a task, and a blank line starts a new paragraph.
DocxXML is what the desktop library stores. It is XML with one element per block, so a table, a callout or an interactive widget survives a round trip without being flattened into text.

pre.caption: The same chapter in DocxXML
pre.code:
One idea per line

A quote can carry the argument.

p: You rarely need to type DocxXML by hand. The editor produces it, the importer reads it, and .mdxb stores it chapter by chapter. The full grammar is in docs/FORMAT.md.

ul.li: Import a Markdown file with ⌘ ⇧ I; it becomes a page in the library.
Export Markdown from the page menu; images and attachments are copied beside it.
Export a book with “Download as → MarkdownX book (.mdxb)” to keep the page tree and every interactive block.

callout.p: A Markdown export is for reading and diffing. Use .mdxb when the book should still be interactive after it leaves your machine.

p: Keep sentences short and avoid idioms that only work in one language. A .mdxb chapter can store an English body in content_en next to the primary Chinese body; the reader switches without reloading the page.
Changing the interface language in Settings does not translate or overwrite existing file names or content.
